q-139070.name: Question 1
q-139070.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x={t}^{3},\,y={2}^{t},\,t\in [0,1].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis?
q-139070.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=1.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3})=3{t}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({2}^{t})={2}^{t}\operatorname{ln}⁡2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{2}^{t}\sqrt{{(3{t}^{2})}^{2}+{({2}^{t}\operatorname{ln}⁡2)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{2}^{t}\sqrt{9{t}^{4}+{2}^{2t}{ln}^{2}⁡2}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{2}^{t}\sqrt{9{t}^{4}+{4}^{t}{ln}^{2}⁡2}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1

Consider the curve defined parametrically as x=t3,y=2t,t∈[0,1]. What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated 2π radians about the x-axis?

a
2π∫01t33t2+2tln⁡2dt
b
6π∫0123tt2dt
c
2π∫012t9t4+4tln2⁡2dt
d
πln⁡2∫012t3t2+2tdt
e
8πln⁡2∫012tt3dt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated 2π radians about the x-axis using the formula

S=∫2πyds.

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

ds=(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt. Therefore, we will use

S=2π∫t1t2y(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt.

We are told that the limits of integration are from t1=0 to t2=1.

Computing the derivatives, we get

dxdt=ddt(t3)=3t2dydt=ddt(2t)=2tln⁡2.

Therefore,

S=2π∫t1t2y(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt=2π∫012t(3t2)2+(2tln⁡2)2dt=2π∫012t9t4+22tln2⁡2dt=2π∫012t9t4+4tln2⁡2dt.

q-139066.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=2t,\,y=3t+2,\,t\in [0,2].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis?
q-139066.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=2.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)=2 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t+2)=3.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated 2π radians about the x-axis using the formula

S=∫2πyds.

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

ds=(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt. Therefore, we will use

S=2π∫t1t2y(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt.

We are told that the limits of integration are from t1=0 to t2=2.

Computing the derivatives, we get

dxdt=ddt(2t)=2dydt=ddt(3t+2)=3.

Therefore,

S=2π∫t1t2y(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt=2π∫02(3t+2)(2)2+(3)2dt=2π∫02(3t+2)13dt=213π∫02(3t+2)dt.

q-139054.name: Question 3
q-139054.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x={t}^{2},\,y=t,\,t\in [0,2].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis?
q-139054.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=2.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})=2t \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{t}^{2}\sqrt{{(2t)}^{2}+{(1)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{t}^{2}\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Consider the curve defined parametrically as x=t2,y=t,t∈[0,2]. What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated 2π radians about the y-axis?

a
4π∫02t3dt
b
2π∫02tt+1dt
c
4π∫02t4dt
d
2π∫02t2+2dt
e
2π∫02t24t2+1dt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated 2π radians about the y-axis using the formula

S=∫2πxds.

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

ds=(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt. Therefore, we will use

S=2π∫t1t2x(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt.

We are told that the limits of integration are from t1=0 to t2=2.

Computing the derivatives, we get

dxdt=ddt(t2)=2tdydt=ddt(t)=1.

Therefore,

S=2π∫t1t2x(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt=2π∫02t2(2t)2+(1)2dt=2π∫02t24t2+1dt.

q-139055.name: Question 4
q-139055.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=t+1,\,y=2{t}^{3},\,t\in [0,1].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis?
q-139055.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=1.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+1)=1 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{3})=6{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(t+1)\sqrt{{(1)}^{2}+{(6{t}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(t+1)\sqrt{1+36{t}^{4}}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

Consider the curve defined parametrically as x=t+1,y=2t3,t∈[0,1]. What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated 2π radians about the y-axis?

a
2π∫01(t+1)1+36t4dt
b
4π∫01t31+36t4dt
c
12π∫01(t+1)t2dt
d
12π∫01t5dt
e
6π∫01t(t+1)1+6t2dt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated 2π radians about the y-axis using the formula

S=∫2πxds.

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

ds=(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt. Therefore, we will use

S=2π∫t1t2x(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt.

We are told that the limits of integration are from t1=0 to t2=1.

Computing the derivatives, we get

dxdt=ddt(t+1)=1dydt=ddt(2t3)=6t2.

Therefore,

S=2π∫t1t2x(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt=2π∫01(t+1)(1)2+(6t2)2dt=2π∫01(t+1)1+36t4dt.

q-352092.name: Question 5
q-352092.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x={e}^{t},\,y=\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}-\frac{t}{4},\,t\in [0,\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)].
$$

Determine the surface area $S$ generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis. Do not round the answer.

$S=$
{{field-1}}
q-352092.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2).$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[{e}^{t}]={e}^{t}, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}-\frac{t}{4}]={e}^{2t}-\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}{e}^{t}\sqrt{{[{e}^{t}]}^{2}+{[{e}^{2t}-\frac{1}{4}]}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}{e}^{t}\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+{e}^{4t}-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}+\frac{1}{16}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}{e}^{t}\sqrt{{e}^{4t}+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}+\frac{1}{16}}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recognizing that the term under the square root is a perfect square, we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}{e}^{t}\sqrt{{({e}^{2t}+\frac{1}{4})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}{e}^{t}({e}^{2t}+\frac{1}{4})\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}({e}^{3t}+\frac{1}{4}{e}^{t})\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}{e}^{t}({e}^{2t}+\frac{1}{4})\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u={e}^{t}.$ Then, $\text{d}u={e}^{t}\,\text{d}t.$  We also update the limits of integration for $u:$

| **$t$** | $0$ | $\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $2$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}{e}^{t}({e}^{2t}+\frac{1}{4})\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}({u}^{2}+\frac{1}{4})\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\pi {[\frac{{u}^{3}}{3}+\frac{u}{4}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =2\pi [(\frac{8}{3}+\frac{2}{4})-(\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{4})] \\  & =2\pi [\frac{7}{3}+\frac{1}{4}] \\  & =2\pi [\frac{28}{12}+\frac{3}{12}] \\  & =2\pi \cdot \frac{31}{12} \\  & =\frac{31\pi }{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-138972.name: Question 6
q-138972.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,y=1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,t\in [0,\pi ].
$$

Calculate the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis.
q-138972.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=\pi .$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{{(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}+{(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{2-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the identity $\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{2}={sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{t}{2}),$ we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{2-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{2(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }2{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{t}{2})\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{t}{2})}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }2{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{t}{2})\cdot |2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{t}{2})|\,\text{d}t \\  & =8\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{t}{2})\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{t}{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & =8\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{t}{2}))\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{t}{2})\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{t}{2}).$ Then, $\text{d}u=-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{t}{2})\,\text{d}t.$ We also need to compute new limits, given below.

| **$t$** | $0$ | $\pi $ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $0$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =8\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{t}{2}))\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{t}{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & =8\pi {\int }_{1}^{0}-2(1-{u}^{2})\,\text{d}u \\  & =16\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(1-{u}^{2})\,\text{d}u \\  & =16\pi \cdot {[u-\frac{{u}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =16\pi (1-\frac{1}{3}-0) \\  & =16\pi (\frac{2}{3}) \\  & =\frac{32\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the curve defined parametrically as x=t−sin⁡t,y=1−cos⁡t,t∈[0,π]. Calculate the surface area generated when this curve is rotated 2π radians about the x-axis.

a
 32π3
b
 12π5
c
 16π5
d
 45π4
e
 64π3
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated 2π radians about the x-axis using the formula

S=∫2πyds.

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

ds=(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt. Therefore, we will use

S=2π∫t1t2y(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt.

We are told that the limits of integration are from t1=0 to t2=π.

Computing the derivatives, we get

dxdt=ddt(t−sin⁡t)=1−cos⁡tdydt=ddt(1−cos⁡t)=sin⁡t.

Therefore,

S=2π∫t1t2y(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt=2π∫0π(1−cos⁡t)(1−cos⁡t)2+(sin⁡t)2dt=2π∫0π(1−cos⁡t)1−2cos⁡t+cos2⁡t+sin2⁡tdt=2π∫0π(1−cos⁡t)1−2cos⁡t+1dt=2π∫0π(1−cos⁡t)2−2cos⁡tdt

Now, using the identity 1−cos⁡t2=sin2⁡(t2), we can rewrite our integral as follows:

S=2π∫0π(1−cos⁡t)2−2cos⁡tdt=2π∫0π(1−cos⁡t)2(1−cos⁡t)dt=2π∫0π2sin2⁡(t2)4sin2⁡(t2)dt=2π∫0π2sin2⁡(t2)⋅|2sin⁡(t2)|dt=8π∫0πsin2⁡(t2)sin⁡(t2)dt=8π∫0π(1−cos2⁡(t2))sin⁡(t2)dt

We evaluate the last integral using the substitution u=cos⁡(t2). Then, du=−12sin⁡(t2)dt. We also need to compute new limits, given below.

t 0 π
u 1 0

Therefore, we get

S=8π∫0π(1−cos2⁡(t2))sin⁡(t2)dt=8π∫10−2(1−u2)du=16π∫01(1−u2)du=16π⋅[u−u33]01=16π(1−13−0)=16π(23)=32π3.
